problemText: You are researching whether after-school sports improve students' grades. What does it mean for a source to be credible when answering this question?
choices: The source was written by someone named, has a way to know the information firsthand, and you understand why they wrote it.
The source has an official-looking website with professional colors and a serious tone, so it appears trustworthy to readers.
The source is the first result when you search for the topic online, meaning search engines ranked it highest.
The source uses lots of statistics and numbers to support its claims, even if you cannot verify where those numbers came from.
hints: Think about the three questions you ask about every source.
Design and appearance are not the same as credibility.

problemText: You find two sources about how many students ride the school bus at Fernbrook Middle. Source 1 is a post on a social media page that says, 'I think most kids here take the bus,' signed by an unknown account. Source 2 is a report on the school district's website, written by the transportation coordinator, with exact counts from the bus roster. Which source is more credible for this question, and why?
choices: Source 1, because it comes from a student who attends the school and experiences the bus system daily.
Source 2, because the transportation coordinator keeps the actual bus records and is named.
Source 1, because social media posts reach more people and represent common opinions held at the school.
Source 2, because it was published on an official website rather than on a social media platform.
hints: Ask yourself who wrote each source and how they would actually know.
Firsthand access to records beats a guess, even from someone inside the school.

problemText: Your research question is: did the new school lunch menu actually reduce food waste? You find a blog post written by a parent who visits the cafeteria once a week and says the trash bins look emptier now. You also find the school's official food-waste report, written by the cafeteria manager, showing the actual weight of food waste measured on a scale before and after the menu change. Which source gives you better evidence for your research question, and what is the main reason?
choices: The parent's blog, because parents have a long history of observing school cafeterias and noticing changes over time.
The parent's blog, because it was written by someone who personally cares about reducing waste in the school.
The cafeteria manager's report, because it is based on what was actually measured and counted, not on how something looked.
The cafeteria manager's report, because managers have official titles and therefore their reports must always be more accurate than parent observations.
hints: Think about how each person would know their information.
A guess about how something looks is not the same as a measured record.

problemText: Your class is researching whether a new bike lane on Maple Street made biking safer. You find three sources. Source A is a comment on the town Facebook page from 'CyclingFan47' (no real name given) saying, 'The new lane is great and way safer.' Source B is a report by the town police department's safety officer listing the number of bike accidents on Maple Street before and after the bike lane was built. Source C is a promotional flyer from BikeCo, a bicycle shop on Maple Street, claiming 'Our bike sales have doubled since the lane opened, which proves it made biking way safer.' Using the three credibility questions, which source or sources would you trust most for this question, and why?
choices: Sources A and C together, because both people are excited about the bike lane, have personal investment in it, and would benefit if more people believe it is safer.
Source B only, because the police officer is named, has direct access to accident records, and has no financial reason to exaggerate the safety gain.
Source C only, because the bike shop owner works right there on Maple Street, observes riders daily, and can speak from firsthand experience about how behavior has changed.
All three equally, because each one provides a different perspective on the bike lane, all three come from people with community ties, and together they offer a complete picture.
hints: For each source, ask who wrote it, how would they know, and what would they gain.
When motives conflict with access to records, the one with actual measurements usually matters more.

problemText: Two sources disagree about how much plastic the school's recycling program actually collects. Source X, from the school facilities manager (who measures the weight on a scale monthly), reports 120 pounds a week. Source Y, from an environmental club flyer, claims recycling 'probably around 300 pounds a week to really help the planet.' The facilities manager does not work for the environmental club and has no reason to hide good numbers. Running the three credibility questions on each source, what does this disagreement tell you?
choices: The disagreement is itself a clue to check how each person knows their number; Source X is more likely to be correct because the facilities manager has direct access to actual weights, while Source Y offers no explanation for how they arrived at 300 pounds.
The disagreement proves that one source must be using a different method of measurement, so you should average the two numbers together to get the most accurate estimate of actual collection.
The disagreement means you cannot determine which number is correct without knowing whether the school's recycling happens every day or just once a week.
The disagreement shows that both groups care about recycling but have estimated differently, so the real number is probably somewhere between 120 and 300 pounds per week.
hints: When sources disagree, run the three questions on each one and compare the answers.
The source with actual, firsthand records usually outweighs the one with a guess or an estimate.

problemText: Your research question is: does the town's new water-conservation program actually save water? You find Source 1: a post by the town mayor on the town website saying the program is 'hugely successful,' but no numbers are given. You find Source 2: a peer-reviewed article by a hydrologist (water scientist) at a university, describing a detailed study of three similar towns over two years, two of which adopted the conservation program and one that did not; the towns with the program used about 15 percent less water on average. You find Source 3: a newsletter from SaveWater Inc., a company that sells water-saving equipment, claiming the program 'cuts water use by up to 50 percent' but offering no details about how they measured this. All three sources are named, but you need to decide which to rely on. Using all three credibility questions plus the idea that disagreement between sources is itself a clue, explain which source or sources give you the strongest evidence and why.
choices: Source 1 is strongest because the mayor holds an elected office and would damage their reputation if they made false claims about a major town program to the public.

Source 2 is strongest because the hydrologist studied multiple towns over time with no financial stake in the outcome, while Source 3 sells equipment and has a motive to exaggerate, and Source 1 gives no measured numbers at all.

Source 3 is strongest because it claims the biggest improvement, represents a company with expertise in water-saving technology, and has likely tested the program more thoroughly than the town itself.

All three are equally credible because they all come from named sources with relevant positions, each one mentions different measurements, and considering all three perspectives together gives the fullest understanding.
hints: Notice what each source gains if readers believe it: does someone make money, win an argument, or just report findings?
When one source has firsthand data from multiple years and towns, and another sells a product related to the claim, the disagreement points to which one to trust.

problemText: A source record has three pieces of information that must be recorded whenever you use a source in your research. Which of the following is one of those three pieces?
choices: How long the source is
The year the source was published
Who made the source
What grade you are in
hints: Think about the three labeled pieces: WHO, WHAT, and WHERE.
You need to be able to find the source again later, so one of these pieces helps identify who created it.

problemText: A student found a book titled 'The Secret Lives of Bees' written by Maria Santos. She wrote in her notes: 'bees and their behavior.' This is a problem with her note. Which piece of the source record did she write incorrectly?
choices: The date—she should have included the year the book was published in her source record
The author—she should have written down Maria Santos's name as the person who wrote the book
The location—she should have noted which publisher or library the book came from
The title—she wrote the topic instead of the exact name printed on the book
hints: Look at what she wrote: 'bees and their behavior.' Compare that to the actual title of the book.
The WHAT piece of a source record must be the exact words printed on the source itself, not a description of what it is about.

problemText: A student watched a documentary video called 'Building Tomorrow's Cities' on a YouTube channel named Urban Design Lab. Inside the video, a city planner named Dr. Jacob Torres explains how modern buildings are designed. The student's note reads: WHO: Dr. Jacob Torres. WHAT: 'Building Tomorrow's Cities.' WHERE: YouTube. Which piece of this source record is incorrect?
choices: The WHO piece—Dr. Torres is interviewed in the video, but the channel Urban Design Lab made and posted it
The WHAT piece—the title should describe what the video is about rather than use the exact printed title
The WHERE piece—YouTube is too vague; the student should have written the exact video URL
The WHERE piece—the student should have written 'Urban Design Lab' instead of 'YouTube'
hints: Remember: the person whose name you hear or see inside a source is not always the person who made it.
Who actually created and posted the video—Dr. Torres or the channel that owns it?

problemText: A student is taking notes on a website article about coral reefs. The website is called Ocean Watch, and she can see the byline 'By Carmen Liu' under the headline 'How Coral Reefs Protect Coastal Communities.' Her current note says only: 'coral article from Ocean Watch.' She wants to make this into a complete basic source record. Which of the following shows what her finished note should include?
choices: WHO: coral reefs, WHAT: 'How Coral Reefs Protect Coastal Communities,' WHERE: Ocean Watch
WHO: Carmen Liu, WHAT: 'How Coral Reefs Protect Coastal Communities,' WHERE: Ocean Watch website
WHO: Ocean Watch, WHAT: 'coastal communities,' WHERE: Carmen Liu's website
WHO: Carmen Liu, WHAT: 'coral article,' WHERE: Ocean Watch.com
hints: Check each of the three pieces: Who wrote it? What is the exact title? Where can someone find it?
The byline tells you the author; the headline gives you the exact title; the website name is where it was found.

problemText: Two students each made a source record for the same magazine article. The article is called 'Why Dogs Bark' by Professor Antonio Riggs, published in Pet Science Today magazine. Read both records below. Student A's record: WHO: Professor Antonio Riggs, WHAT: 'Why Dogs Bark,' WHERE: Pet Science Today magazine. Student B's record: WHO: Pet Science Today, WHAT: Why Dogs Bark, WHERE: Riggs.com. Which student created a correct source record, and why?
choices: Both students are correct because they both identified the article's author, title, and magazine, just organized differently in their records
Student B is correct because the magazine name belongs in WHO since it is the organization responsible for publishing the article online
Student A is correct because the author's name goes in WHO, the exact title with quotation marks goes in WHAT, and the magazine name goes in WHERE
Neither student is correct because they both failed to include additional details such as the publication date or page number of the article
hints: Check Student A's record piece by piece: Does the author go in WHO? Is the title written exactly as printed? Is the place clear?
Check Student B: Did the student confuse who made the article with where it was published? Is the title missing proper punctuation?

problemText: A student found three different sources and wrote them down quickly without thinking about completeness. Source 1: 'National Geographic—animals sleeping.' Source 2: AUTHOR: Kenji Honda, TITLE: 'How Plants Grow,' FOUND: textbook. Source 3: WHO: WKID News Station, WHAT: 'Five-Day Weather Report,' WHERE: WKID's local TV channel. The student must submit one source record that is complete and correct. Which source would need the most work to fix into a proper source record, and what is the main problem?
choices: All three sources have equal amounts of missing information so the student cannot fix any of them
Source 2 needs the most work because the author's name is missing the first initial and the textbook page number is not included
Source 3 needs the most work because TV channels cannot be considered sources for a school research project
Source 1 needs the most work because it has no author, writes the topic instead of the title, and lacks a clear place
hints: Look at Source 1 carefully: How many of the three pieces (WHO, WHAT, WHERE) are actually there? What did the student write instead of the real title?
Sources 2 and 3 both have all three pieces labeled and in roughly the right place—Source 1 is missing an author entirely.

problemText: A student writes down the word 'dinosaurs' on a piece of paper for a short research project. The teacher asks, 'Do you have a research question yet?' Why would the teacher ask this question?
choices: Because 'dinosaurs' needs to be combined with other words to form a complete sentence structure
Because 'dinosaurs' is a topic, not a research question, and it does not tell the student what specific information they actually want to find out
Because the student must decide on a narrower subject area within dinosaurs before they can begin any kind of research work
Because 'dinosaurs' is a topic, not a research question, and it does not tell the student when the project will be finished
hints: A topic is something you could read about forever without finishing.
A research question must end with a question mark and name exactly what you want to find out.

problemText: Jordan is researching mountains for a two-page report. He narrows his topic to 'How do mountains form?' and writes it down as his research question. When Jordan searches for this question, he finds that almost every source gives him the same basic answer: plate tectonics cause mountains to form over millions of years. What does this tell Jordan about his research question?
choices: His question is too narrow because one main idea from sources answers it almost completely, leaving little for a two-page report
His question is perfect because every source he finds happens to discuss the same answer in a straightforward way
His question is too broad because it would require him to read about every single mountain range that exists on Earth and how each one formed
His question fails because it asks about events that happened millions of years ago and cannot be studied using modern scientific methods
hints: A research question should need several sources that you gather pieces from and put together.
If your first source already answers the whole question, you may need to add more limits to make it deeper.

problemText: A student is writing about the history of soccer. She is deciding between two questions: 'When was soccer first played?' and 'How has the way players pass a soccer ball changed over the last fifty years?' Which question would work better as a real research question for a short project, and why?
choices: 'When was soccer first played?' because it is easier to find the answer in a single reliable source and does not require pulling together information from different places
'How has the way players pass a soccer ball changed over the last fifty years?' because it asks about a change that requires comparing information from multiple sources instead of looking up one fact

'How has the way players pass a soccer ball changed over the last fifty years?' because it focuses on a specific sport skill rather than the sport in general and can be answered by looking at historical video or coaching documents
'When was soccer first played?' because questions about dates are more important and more valued in research projects than questions about techniques and are considered factual
hints: A question that has only one fact behind it is a lookup, not a real research project.
A research question needs you to gather pieces from several sources and put them together.

problemText: Kenji wants to research artificial intelligence for his project. He starts with the question 'Is artificial intelligence good or bad?' but then realizes there is a problem with it. Kenji decides to change his question to 'What are the differences in how fast humans and computers solve math problems?' Explain what was wrong with Kenji's first question and why his new question is better, using the three tests for a strong research question.
choices: The first question asks about too many types of artificial intelligence and lacks focus, while the new question fixes this by asking only about math problems and solving speed. However, the new question may still be too broad because it could take a whole book to answer it completely.
The first question has too many words, and the new question is shorter. The new question is better because shorter questions are always easier to research and require less time to complete.

The first question asks for a judgment that people could disagree about even after reading the same sources, while the new question asks what evidence can measure and compare. The new question is also narrow enough (one type of task) and broad enough (needs sources on human and computer abilities).

The first question cannot be answered by any source at all because it is too vague, while the new question can be answered with concrete data. The new question is also better because it uses simpler words than the first question.
hints: A research question must be answerable by evidence, not by what someone prefers or believes should happen.
A strong question is narrow enough for your project size, broad enough to need several sources, and settled by facts rather than opinions.

problemText: Lucia is researching sleep for a three-page project. Her first question is 'Why do teenagers need more sleep than adults?' She searches for sources and finds many articles from sleep scientists about the differences in teen and adult sleep needs. However, after reading three sources, Lucia realizes they all point to the same basic answer: teenage brains are still developing and require more rest. Lucia decides to refocus her question to 'How does the amount of sleep a teenager gets affect their performance in school the next day?' What is Lucia doing by making this change, and what test was her original question failing?
choices: Lucia is refocusing because her first question failed the evidence test—it was asking for an opinion instead of a fact that could be proven with research.
Lucia is narrowing her question to make it harder to answer, which will force her to use more sources and do more work than she originally planned.
Lucia is making her question worse because she is no longer asking about sleep itself, which was her original topic, and has shifted to asking about school performance instead.

Lucia is widening her question because her first question was too narrow—it had one clear answer sitting in sources, not enough to fill three pages. Her new question asks about a cause and effect that requires pulling together pieces from different sources.
hints: If your first source already answers the whole question, it was too narrow, a single fact after all, and you can widen it back out.
Refocusing means adjusting your question after you start searching, either by narrowing it further or by loosening a limit that made it too small.

problemText: A student is researching the history of medicine for a four-page project. She writes three possible questions: (1) 'What are the main ways antibiotics have changed since they were discovered?' (2) 'Should doctors prescribe antibiotics when patients ask for them?' (3) 'In what year were antibiotics invented?' She wants to pick one question that will pass all three tests. For each question, identify which test or tests it fails, and explain why it fails that test. Which question, if any, would actually work for her project?
choices: Question 1 is the only one that works because it asks about changes (which requires multiple sources), limits the topic (antibiotics, not all medicine), and asks about facts evidence can show. Question 2 fails the evidence test (asks what should happen, a judgment). Question 3 fails the broad-enough test (one fact in one place).

Question 2 is the only one that works because it requires a student to think deeply about ethics and different viewpoints from multiple research sources and allows for personal interpretation of the evidence.
Question 3 is the only one that works because it can be answered quickly from an encyclopedia or history of science article without needing multiple sources and provides a simple, factual answer.
All three questions work equally well because they are all written as complete questions with question marks and could potentially be researched using books or websites on medical history.
hints: Remember the three tests: narrow enough for the space, broad enough to need more than one source, and answerable by evidence not personal preference.
A question that asks what should happen or what is best is a judgment, not a fact, and no source can prove one person right when others disagree.

problemText: A quote copies a source's exact words and sets them off in quotation marks. A paraphrase rebuilds an idea from a source in your own words and sentence structure while keeping the meaning the same. Which statement correctly describes what makes these two moves different?
choices: A quote is shorter than a paraphrase and works better in most reports.
A quote keeps the exact wording and uses quotation marks; a paraphrase changes the wording but rebuilds the sentence shape too.
A paraphrase uses quotation marks to show it came from a source; a quote does not need them.
A quote is used when you want to summarize the main idea; a paraphrase is used when the exact words matter.
hints: Think about what quotation marks signal to a reader.
Remember: a paraphrase does not just swap in synonyms — it rebuilds the whole sentence.

problemText: You are writing a report on how plants grow, and you find this sentence in a gardening book: 'Sunlight helps plants make their own food through a process called photosynthesis.' You want to use the general idea that sunlight helps plants make food, but you do not need the exact wording or the word 'photosynthesis.' Which choice is a fair paraphrase of this sentence?
choices: Sunlight assists plants in making their own food by means of photosynthesis.
Sunlight helps plants make their own food through a process called photosynthesis.
Plants rely on sunlight to produce the energy and nutrients they need to grow.
Sunlight helps plants make their own food, which is called photosynthesis.
hints: A real paraphrase does not just swap a few words into the same sentence order.
Look for an answer that rebuilds the idea in a completely new sentence shape.

problemText: You are writing a report and want to include this exact sentence from a wildlife magazine: 'Wolves live and hunt in packs because the group makes them stronger hunters.' You decide the exact wording matters and you want to quote it. Which choice correctly includes this quote inside your report?
choices: The wildlife magazine states: Wolves live and hunt in packs because the group makes them stronger hunters.
According to the wildlife magazine, wolves live and hunt in packs because the group makes them stronger hunters.
Wolves live and hunt in packs because the group makes them stronger hunters, as the wildlife magazine says.
The wildlife magazine explains that 'wolves live and hunt in packs because the group makes them stronger hunters.'
hints: Remember: quotation marks must wrap around the source's exact words so a reader can see they are not yours.
Check which choice puts the exact words inside quotation marks and names the source.

problemText: A student is writing a report on honey production and finds this sentence in a book about bees: 'A single bee colony can produce up to sixty pounds of honey in one year.' The student writes: 'A lone bee colony is able to generate up to sixty pounds of honey within one year.' The student did not use quotation marks and did not name the source. Why is this a problem, and what should the student do to fix it?
choices: The student swapped in a few different words but kept the source's exact sentence order and meaning, so this is a word-swap copy, not a real paraphrase. The student must either put quotation marks around the exact words and credit the source, or rebuild the sentence completely in new words and new structure, then credit the source.

The student paraphrased correctly but forgot to add quotation marks and the source name, so the student should simply add both of those elements without changing the sentence itself to fix the problem.

The student did not copy enough of the original words to show where the idea came from, so the student should copy more of the exact wording and then put quotation marks around it to properly credit the source.
The student changed the word order too much and made the meaning confusing, so the student should keep the original sentence order while adding quotation marks and a source credit to make it clear.
hints: Look at what the student actually did: did they rebuild the idea from scratch, or did they just trade in a few synonyms?
A word-swap copy needs fixing whether or not quotation marks are added — the real problem is the sentence structure stayed the same.

problemText: You are writing a report about ocean life and find two sentences in a marine biology guide: 'Most fish use gills to breathe underwater. Gills take oxygen from the water so the fish can use it.' You want to use both ideas but you do not need the exact wording. You plan to paraphrase both sentences together into one new sentence. Which choice correctly paraphrases both ideas without word-swapping and also credits the source?
choices: The marine biology guide says that most fish use gills to breathe underwater, and gills take oxygen from the water so the fish can use it.
According to the marine biology guide, fish rely on gills as the body part that pulls oxygen from water and allows them to breathe beneath the surface.
Fish use gills to breathe underwater because gills take oxygen from water, as the marine biology guide explains.
Most fish use gills to take oxygen from water so they can breathe, according to the guide.
hints: A real paraphrase combines the two ideas into a new sentence shape, not the source's original order.
Watch for choices that keep the source's sentences or sentence order almost exactly — those are word-swaps, not paraphrases.

problemText: A student found this sentence in a history book about medieval castles: 'Castle walls were built thick and tall to protect the people inside from enemy attacks.' The student wrote three different versions. Version 1: 'Castle walls were built thick and tall to protect the people inside from enemy attacks.' Version 2: 'Castle walls were constructed thick and tall to shield the people within from enemy assaults.' Version 3: 'To defend the people who lived inside, medieval castles had thick, tall walls.' Only Version 3 has quotation marks and credits the source. Which statement correctly explains which version or versions need fixing and why?
choices: Version 2 is correct because it changes enough words to make it the student's own work. Versions 1 and 3 need quotation marks.
Only Version 1 needs fixing because it copies the source word for word. Versions 2 and 3 are both acceptable paraphrases.

Versions 1 and 2 both need fixing because they use the source's exact words or sentence order without quotation marks. Version 3 is correct because it rebuilds the idea in new words and structure, then credits the source.
All three versions need quotation marks because they all came from a source, whether the student changed the words or not.
hints: Remember: a word-swap (keeping the same sentence structure but trading in synonyms) is not a real paraphrase and is still a problem even without quotation marks.
A real paraphrase must rebuild the sentence from scratch in both words and structure. Which version actually does that?
